Al-Rāzī reports ʿAlī and Ibn ʿUmar reading the command as 'Glory be to my Lord, the Most High' followed by the relative clause; he says it supplies the words of glorification."}]}
{"id": "87:2/q15", "question": "What reported recitation or prayer events involve this passage or its sūra?", "turns_on": "These are separate reports about prostration, an addition to recitation, and the Prophet's customary sūra recitation.", "positions": [{"id": "87:2/q15/p1", "position": "The Prophet instructed 'Glory be to my Lord, the Most High' in prostration after this sūra's opening.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī cites ʿUqba ibn ʿĀmir, who also reports 'Glory be to my Lord, the Great' in bowing after 56:74. Al-Durr reports Abū Hurayra's account that the Companions asked what to say in prostration and then the sūra was revealed."}, {"id": "87:2/q15/p2", "position": "The Prophet told Ḥaḍramī to add nothing after he appended his own line about a pregnant woman to the recited verses.", "reasons": "Al-Durr reports Ḥaḍramī ibn ʿĀmir's recitation and the Prophet's judgment that it was sufficient as given."}, {"id": "87:2/q15/p3", "position": "The Prophet loved the sūra and recited it with al-Ghāshiya at Eid and Friday prayers, sometimes on one day.", "reasons": "Qutb cites ʿAlī on the Prophet's love and Muslim on the paired recitation with sūra 88; he also says al-Aʿlā is Meccan and has nineteen verses."}]}
{"id": "87:2/q16", "question": "How does the following determination develop the account of creation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:2/q16/p1", "position": "The following verb can be read as 'measured' or as 'had power' or 'determined,' affirming God's direct power over what He created.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports qaddara and qadara as variant readings and explains the latter by God's continuing direct power over creation."}]}
{"id": "87:2/q17", "question": "What guidance follows God's creating and fashioning?", "turns_on": "Whether guidance denotes creatures' instinct for nourishment or human religious guidance by signs and proofs.", "positions": [{"id": "87:2/q17/p1", "position": "Creatures have instinctive guidance toward their allotted nourishment.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports this as one meaning of the following guidance."}, {"id": "87:2/q17/p2", "position": "God leads people to religion and knowledge of His unity through signs and proofs.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports this as another meaning of the following guidance."}]}
{"id": "87:3/q01", "question": "How is قَدَّرَ read?", "turns_on": "Whether the light form merely shares the doubled form's sense or also conveys ability or ownership.", "positions": [{"id": "87:3/q01/p1", "position": "The majority double the dāl, reading qaddara.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ and al-Ṭabarī prefer this by the readers' agreement or consensus. Ibn ʿAṭiyya allows decree or measured proportion; al-Qurṭubī relates it to estimation (25:2). Al-Samīn and Rāzī compare the forms in 77:23."}, {"id": "87:3/q01/p2", "position": "Al-Kisāʾī reads the dāl lightly, qadara; reports also attribute it to ʿAlī and al-Sulamī.", "reasons": "Al-Kisāʾī is called the sole reader among the canonical readers; al-Farrāʾ attributes al-Sulamī's form to ʿAlī. Al-Baghawī, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Wāḥidī, and Ibn ʿĀshūr say the two forms mean the same. Jishumī allows a distinction between power and apportionment; al-Qaffāl reads the light form as ownership and governance; Abū Ḥayyān and Ālūsī mention power or measure; Qirāʾāt-ER lists measuring, determining, estimating, or ability; Study Quran says it may affirm God's direct power over creation."}]}
{"id": "87:3/q02", "question": "What does قَدَّرَ mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the determination names the universal assignment of measure or a particular allotted feature; the light reading also permits power or ownership.", "positions": [{"id": "87:3/q02/p1", "position": "God assigned each created thing its particular measure, properties, capacities, acts, circumstances, and destiny.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī cites 15:21 and lists essence, size, duration, place, beauty, guidance and misguidance. Elmalılı cites 65:3 and 15:21, stressing divine knowledge and will and the unknown secret of destiny; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī describes particular existence arising from an undetermined plenitude and cites 15:21, 54:49, 25:2, 57:22, and 64:11. Ibn ʿĀshūr says measure starts with length, capacity, weight, or count and here means ordered organs and powers. Al-Biqāʿī gives hand, leg, ear, and eye examples. Al-Bayḍāwī, Bursawī, and Ālūsī include kinds, species, individuals, qualities, acts, and lifespans."}, {"id": "87:3/q02/p2", "position": "It means forming or shaping a creature, especially in the womb.", "reasons": "Al-Dāmghānī calls it shaping well in the womb; al-Māwardī describes formation there and emergence fully formed. Study Quran reports the human-specific account of forming the first human after breathing in the Spirit and providing nourishment."}, {"id": "87:3/q02/p3", "position": "It means assigning a particular provision, sustenance, or useful benefit.", "reasons": "ʿAṭāʾ says every animal receives what suits it; al-Wāḥidī's additional report has God determine the offspring He wills. The accounts of livelihood distinguish assigned food from God's placement of useful properties in things."}, {"id": "87:3/q02/p4", "position": "It means determining males and females and their reproductive course.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī says God determined male and female animal forms; Muqātil and al-Kalbī pair that with the guidance of mating. Ibn ʿĀshūr treats reproductive powers as preserving the species."}, {"id": "87:3/q02/p5", "position": "It means fixing gestation, including a term of about nine months with possible variation.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī's report in al-Thaʿlabī and al-Qurṭubī specifies nine months, less, or more; other transmitters state only the allotted period until birth."}, {"id": "87:3/q02/p6", "position": "It means decreeing felicity and misery, or sins followed by repentance.", "reasons": "Mujāhid and al-Wāsiṭī describe assigned destinies; Tustarī distinguishes God's care for the felicitous from leaving the wretched to themselves. Al-Sulamī separately reports allotted sins followed by repentance."}, {"id": "87:3/q02/p7", "position": "It means creating people for recompense.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī's fifth possibility pairs this creation with guidance to action."}, {"id": "87:3/q02/p8", "position": "Other lexical senses include making or appointing, knowing, and the light form's power or ownership.", "reasons": "Al-Dāmghānī lists making or appointing and knowledge without examples in the excerpt. Al-Qaffāl derives the light reading as owning and governing what God creates; al-Qurṭubī also allows possession, while Abū Ḥayyān and Ālūsī mention power. Qirāʾāt-ER gives measuring, determining, estimating, and ability."}]}
{"id": "87:3/q03", "question": "What is God said to guide creatures toward?", "turns_on": "Whether the phrase is unrestricted or names a particular kind of guidance, and whether religious guidance is read as its principal sense.", "positions": [{"id": "87:3/q03/p1", "position": "Every creature is guided toward its allotted function, course, or benefit; particular examples do not limit the verse.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Abū Ḥayyān, Ālūsī, and Elmalılı expressly keep the scope general. Al-Ṭabarī cites lack of evidence for restriction; Elmalılı cites 20:50. Al-Bayḍāwī, al-Biqāʿī, and Bursawī name inclination, inspiration, signs, and revelation. Ibn ʿĀshūr gives speech, craft, grazing, nursing, and bee architecture; al-Biqāʿī says ordainment needs guidance for completeness. Elmalılı includes planetary orbits, attraction, gases, stones, crystals, salt, coal, and cells. Qutb says provision accompanies creatures throughout life; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites 15:21, 80:20, and 2:148."}, {"id": "87:3/q03/p2", "position": "People are shown good and evil, right and error, felicity and misery; livestock are guided to pasture.", "reasons": "Mujāhid's versions vary between assigned misery or happiness and showing moral alternatives. Al-Rāzī connects the latter to perception and the ability to seek benefit and avoid harm, citing 76:3 and 91:7–8. Al-Zajjāj says the person may prove grateful or ungrateful."}, {"id": "87:3/q03/p3", "position": "God directs each person along the felicity or misery already allotted to that person.", "reasons": "Tustarī says God takes charge of the felicitous and leaves the wretched to themselves; al-Wāsiṭī says each group follows its assigned path. These reports describe an outcome, while other Mujāhid reports describe moral alternatives."}, {"id": "87:3/q03/p4", "position": "God directs males and females, especially animals, in how to mate.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī's preferred explanation says each male finds a female of its own species and learns the species-specific manner of mating; ʿAṭāʾ and al-Qurṭubī compare 20:50. Ibn Qutayba calls the direction inspiration. Ibn ʿĀshūr treats reproductive powers as preserving species."}, {"id": "87:3/q03/p5", "position": "The fetus is guided out of the womb at the completion of its allotted term.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī specifies approximately nine months, sometimes shorter or longer. Al-Māwardī also says the child emerges fully formed."}, {"id": "87:3/q03/p6", "position": "Creatures are guided to seek their apportioned livelihood, and animals to their food or pasture.", "reasons": "ʿAṭāʾ and Abū Muslim say every animal receives a fitting provision; al-Zamakhsharī and al-Nasafī add that God teaches its use. Al-Rāzī says God cares for them. Al-Qumm

Al-Biqāʿī notes the newborn's instinctive opening of its mouth; Iṣlāḥī pairs implanted need with means and capacity."}, {"id": "87:3/q03/p9", "position": "Humans are led to religion, faith, monotheism, and right conduct through reason, signs, revelation, or prophetic invitation.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAlī connects forms and livelihood with knowledge of unity; Jishumī includes lifespans, signs, and completed reason. Qatāda distinguishes God's command and approval of obedience from sin. Iṣlāḥī joins moral awareness and prophetic guidance to trials and consequences."}, {"id": "87:3/q03/p10", "position": "God guides sinners to repentance after allotting their sins.", "reasons": "Al-Sulamī reports this formulation; al-Thaʿlabī and Ibn al-Jawzī transmit it among other views."}, {"id": "87:3/q03/p11", "position": "Some are guided to trust God's guarantee quietly instead of striving for their apportioned provisions.", "reasons": "Al-Sulamī contrasts this with the reported view that people are guided to seek their provisions."}, {"id": "87:3/q03/p12", "position": "People are created for recompense and guided to action.", "reasons": "This is al-Māwardī's fifth possibility."}, {"id": "87:3/q03/p13", "position": "People are guided to perceive and use their endowed faculties and capacities.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī describes bodily components fitted to receive faculties and guidance creating the faculties in organs for their beneficial acts. Ibn ʿĀshūr gives a human-specific possibility: completed faculties followed by perception and reason. Study Quran reports a reading of the preceding 'created' as humans specifically, humans and animals, or all creation."}, {"id": "87:3/q03/p14", "position": "God's acts themselves direct rational observers to recognize His oneness, knowledge, power, and majesty.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī lists oneness, majesty, self-sufficiency, and uniqueness; al-Qurṭubī lists oneness, knowledge, and power."}, {"id": "87:3/q03/p15", "position": "Guidance includes explaining the way and God's protective care.", "reasons": "Tustarī differentiates explanation from God's taking charge and uses infant sustenance as the case of care; al-Naḥḥās reports the gloss that God makes matters clear."}]}
{"id": "87:3/q04", "question": "Does فَهَدَىٰ also imply 'led astray'?", "turns_on": "Whether the single named act conventionally carries its opposite by ellipsis.", "positions": [{"id": "87:3/q04/p1", "position": "Yes; 'led astray' is left unspoken because guidance evokes its opposite.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj's grammarians cite 14:4; al-Rāzī and al-Qurṭubī compare 16:81, which names protection from heat without naming cold; al-Nasafī cites 16:93 and 35:8. Al-Farrāʾ is repeatedly named as proponent."}, {"id": "87:3/q04/p2", "position": "No; the proposed ellipsis is rejected.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī explicitly rejects al-Farrāʾ's proposal and prefers the verse's general account of positive guidance."}]}
{"id": "87:3/q05", "question": "Is God said to compel or command misguidance?", "turns_on": "Whether directing to, mentioning, or decreeing error entails compelling or commanding it.", "positions": [{"id": "87:3/q05/p1", "position": "No; God commands and approves obedience while forbidding sin and misguidance.", "reasons": "Qatāda says God neither compels nor commands sin and does not approve it, answering any reading of guidance that would make Him do so."}, {"id": "87:3/q05/p2", "position": "The verse's guidance can include a path to error or an implied act of leading astray.", "reasons": "Mujāhid's reports say God guides toward good and evil or right and error; al-Farrāʾ proposes the implicit opposite. These sources do not all make the same claim about compulsion."}]}

{"id": "87:3/q07", "question": "Who is the unspoken object of فَهَدَىٰ?", "turns_on": "Whether general wording encompasses all created things or only beings capable of apprehending direction.", "positions": [{"id": "87:3/q07/p1", "position": "It is left general, then contextually limited to creatures able to apprehend direction.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr includes humans and animals with perception and will but excludes fruiting trees and seed production, which he calls determined rather than guided."}, {"id": "87:3/q07/p2", "position": "The created object may be humans, humans and animals, or all creation.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports these possibilities for 'created' in the preceding verse; Ibn ʿĀshūr gives the corresponding human-specific reading of determination and guidance."}]}
{"id": "87:3/q08", "question": "How are divine attributes linked by the conjunctions and relative pronoun?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:3/q08/p1", "position": "The repeated relative pronoun and conjunction emphasize distinct divine predicates.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the repetition amplification. {"id": "87:3/q09", "question": "Do the perfect verbs describe only completed past acts?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:3/q09/p1", "position": "No; their perfect form is aspectual, and divine creation is ongoing and sustaining.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum points to the repeated growth and decay of pasture in verses 4–5 and compares 53:43–49, 96:1–5, and 95:4–5."}]}
{"id": "87:3/q10", "question": "What inward guidance does the verse describe?", "turns_on": "Which spiritual stage or disposition the guidance addresses.", "positions": [{"id": "87:3/q10/p1", "position": "Heedless people build the world, while worshippers prefer the afterlife.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī contrasts the objects of their efforts."}, {"id": "87:3/q10/p2", "position": "Ascetics recognize the world's passing nature and reject it.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī gives this as another degree of guidance."}, {"id": "87:3/q10/p3", "position": "Scholars contemplate created signs and remain with their inferences.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī says they recognize God through examining His signs and creation."}, {"id": "87:3/q10/p4", "position": "Seekers turn toward the glory of God's attribute and devote themselves to Him.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī says they prefer Him and expend their effort seeking Him."}, {"id": "87:3/q10/p5", "position": "Gnostics enter the sanctity of His description, watching and then witnessing Him.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī portrays successive stages of awareness."}, {"id": "87:3/q10/p6", "position": "Monotheists abandon familiar things and seek God alone in His sovereign sublimity.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī names this as a distinct orientation."}, {"id": "87:3/q10/p7", "position": "Knowers finally rest in incapacity before God beyond proof, explanation, vision, separation, and union.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī locates the divine beyond these modes."}, {"id": "87:3/q10/p8", "position": "God plants human perfection within a person and guides its actualization through purification.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says refinement brings the potential perfection forth."}]}

{"id": "87:3/q12", "question": "How does this verse support the call to glorify God and relate to the surrounding sūras?", "turns_on": "Which surrounding passage or theological purpose supplies the connection.", "positions": [{"id": "87:3/q12/p1", "position": "Creation, proportion, determination, and guidance display God's power, wisdom, and worthiness of glorification.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says they answer how the Lord is known and why He merits praise; Abraham's words in 26:78, Moses' reply in 20:49–50, and the first revelation in 96:1–4 use the same proof. The wonders are abundant and observable. Al-Qurṭubī's teacher says the clauses show divine exaltedness. Elmalılı says finite creatures imply the Lord's transcendence and grounds for trust amid disbelievers' schemes."}, {"id": "87:3/q12/p2", "position": "The verse's acts counter the disbelievers' schemes and prepare the Prophet for his mission.", "reasons": "Jishumī connects it with the preceding warning; al-Biqāʿī and Ibn al-Zubayr tie the plot in 86:15 to God's power and wisdom in 87:1–3. Iṣlāḥī says al-Ṭāriq promises only temporary respite and this sūra turns to reassure the Prophet. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the One who shaped him will secure his retention of revelation and ease his law (87:6, 87:8)."}, {"id": "87:3/q12/p3", "position": "The verse parallels other statements that creation is measured and creatures directed.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr cites Moses' 20:50 and the predestination report; Asad links 25:2 and 20:50. Corpus Coranicum links qaddara to 80:19 and hadā to 93:7; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites 15:21, 80:20, and 2:148."}, {"id": "87:3/q12/p4", "position": "The ordered creation described in the verse bears on the sūra's themes of oneness, revelation, and recompense.", "reasons": "Qutb describes the cosmos as a place of praise, the Prophet's preservation and ease, and the message's roots in earlier scriptures; Study Quran says creation is properly formed without flaw and cites 67:3–4."}]}

{"id": "87:3/q17", "question": "How does varying related Qur'anic expressions convey meaning?", "turns_on": "Which purpose of expressive variation is being discussed.", "positions": [{"id": "87:3/q17/p1", "position": "Taṣrīf expresses one meaning through varied, connected meanings and forms, clarifying it from several sides.", "reasons": "Al-Rummānī illustrates derivatives of ملك, from owner to king and dominion, and عرض, from appearance and turning away to poetic meter; the linked senses illuminate a shared core."}, {"id": "87:3/q17/p2", "position": "The varied telling of Moses' story sustains eloquence, strengthens admonition, and resolves doubts about the miracle.", "reasons": "Al-Rummānī names al-Aʿrāf, Ṭā Hā, and al-Shuʿarāʾ and gives these three purposes."}, {"id": "87:3/q17/p3", "position": "Variation at the highest eloquent level demonstrates the Qur'anic challenge because God can produce its like.", "reasons": "Al-Rummānī contrasts meaningful challenges within possibility with impossible alternatives such as five times five being other than twenty-five or one hundred having a different unique square root."}]}

{"id": "87:6/q01", "question": "What does “We shall make you recite” mean?", "turns_on": "Whether iqraʾa here is teaching recitation generally or listening for correction.", "positions": [{"id": "87:6/q01/p1", "position": "God will teach Muhammad the Qur’an and make him a reciter.", "reasons": "Baghawī and Thaʿlabī specify Gabriel’s recitation; Mālik, transmitted by Ibn Wahb in Qurṭubī, glosses it as teaching and retention. Nasafī’s shorter note awkwardly says 'until he forgets,' while its full version says 'until he does not forget.'"}, {"id": "87:6/q01/p2", "position": "Iqraʾa can mean receiving a reading by listening so errors can be corrected.", "reasons": "Jishumī and Ṭabrisī also derive qirāʾa from gathering letters. {"id": "87:6/q02", "question": "How will God make the Prophet recite?", "turns_on": "Whether the divine making occurs through Gabriel’s instruction, inspiration, special memory, or an inward reading.", "positions": [{"id": "87:6/q02/p1", "position": "Gabriel conveys and recites the revelation, and God enables Muhammad to retain and deliver it.", "reasons": "Zajjāj says the unlettered Prophet teaches his companions without needing repetition. {"id": "87:6/q06", "question": "What does “forget” mean here in Arabic usage?", "turns_on": "The lexical sense and vocalization of nisyān.", "positions": [{"id": "87:6/q06/p1", "position": "It is the opposite of remembering: known information fails to come to mind, briefly or for long.", "reasons": "Damghānī cites 18:63 and 18:73 and glosses this verse as lasting retention. {"id": "87:6/q07", "question": "What is the nature of forgetting?", "turns_on": "Whether forgetting is a created act or a privation of knowledge.", "positions": [{"id": "87:6/q07/p1", "position": "Forgetting is an act created by God.", "reasons": "Jishumī reports Abū ʿAlī; Ṭabrisī attributes the point to Abū ʿAlī al-Jubbāʾī."}, {"id": "87:6/q07/p2", "position": "Forgetting is the loss of ordinarily necessary knowledge, not an entity or act.", "reasons": "Jishumī reports Abū Hāshim in disagreement with Abū ʿAlī."}]}
{"id": "87:6/q08", "question": "Is “you will not forget” a statement or a prohibition?", "turns_on": "Whether lā negates a predicted event or prohibits an avoidable cause of forgetting; the retained final alif also matters.", "positions": [{"id": "87:6/q08/p1", "position": "It is an asserted negation that functions as God’s promise of preserved memory.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās prefers exegetical support and says most linguists reject commanding involuntary forgetting.
